question: Under fixed capacity, how does increasing allocation to a fifth family affect that family and the already-learned families across prior-order conditions?
observed: Equal-mass fifth-family integrated performance was about 0.749 to 0.751 across the tested prior orders.
Increasing fifth-family allocation raised fifth-family integrated performance, reaching about 0.796 at the 1.5-mass allocation.
All-family integrated performance stayed roughly in the 0.765 to 0.769 range while minimum-family performance could fall, showing competition rather than free capacity gain.
The qualification harness classified the run as a qualified scientific result.
established: Under the tested fixed-capacity regime, allocating more mass to the fifth family improves that family while redistributing performance pressure across prior families.
The capacity/plasticity tradeoff persists across the tested prior-order variants.
not_established: The result does not establish an allocation that is globally optimal for every family.
The result does not establish unbounded continual learning.
frozen_constraints: Keep total capacity and the tested prior-order conditions fixed when attributing allocation effects.
Do not reinterpret family gains without accounting for minimum-family and all-family performance.
next_seams: Test whether consolidation/history mechanisms can reduce the fixed-capacity competition without adding capacity.
